name: Insilico Medicine and End-to-End AI Platforms
blurb: The company with the most advanced fully AI derived drug.
title: Insilico Medicine and End-to-End AI Platforms
answer: Insilico Medicine used AI both to choose the target, TNIK, and to design the molecule, rentosertib, for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Its phase 2a trial showed a gain in lung function against decline on placebo, published in Nature Medicine in 2025, and the company has moved the drug toward a phase 3 trial.

reading.body:
Rentosertib is the clearest evidence so far that AI can carry a drug from target selection to a clinical signal, but it is not yet evidence that the drug works.

Insilico's platform chose the target, TNIK, and designed the molecule. In a phase 2a trial published in Nature Medicine in 2025, mean forced vital capacity rose 98.4 mL on the top dose over 12 weeks while placebo declined 20.3 mL. That is a small, short trial, and its value is as a signal rather than proof. The company has since initiated a phase 3 trial.

The pattern worth noting is end to end: the same organization proposed the biology and generated the chemistry, rather than licensing a molecule or handing a target to a partner. That compresses the earliest, most failure-prone stage of drug development, where most candidates die before reaching patients. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has few treatment options, so a lung function gain against decline is the outcome that matters.

What the data does not cover is compute. No training runs, chip counts, data center capacity, or power figures appear here, so nothing can be said about what this pipeline costs to run or whether it is constrained by hardware. It also does not establish a success rate for AI derived drugs, because one candidate in one phase 2a trial cannot produce one. Phase 3 will decide whether the target holds up at scale. Until then the proven claim is speed to the clinic, not the odds of approval.

siblings.name: Frontier AI Models Built for Biology
Lab Automation and the Lab in the Loop

explainer:
Insilico Medicine built an end to end platform: one system analyses biological data to propose new targets, another generates molecules against them, and a third helps plan trials. Rentosertib is the best known result. Its target, an enzyme called TNIK, was nominated by the company's target discovery AI as a driver of fibrosis, and the molecule was designed with its generative chemistry system.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive scarring of the lungs with few treatment options, so lung function measured as forced vital capacity is the key outcome. In the phase 2a trial, patients on the highest dose improved while those on placebo declined over 12 weeks. A phase 2a trial is small and short, so its main value is as a signal; the larger phase 3 trial will decide whether the drug works and is safe enough to approve.

What end to end means

Most AI drug discovery companies specialise in one step: finding targets, designing molecules or predicting properties. Insilico Medicine built a connected platform that covers the sequence from target discovery, through generative chemistry that designs molecules against the target, to tools that predict trial outcomes, and it has used that platform on its own pipeline rather than only as a service. That is what makes it the most watched test of whether an integrated AI approach can produce medicines.

What it has shown

The company's lead programme, for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, was the first candidate with both an AI discovered target and an AI designed molecule to reach phase 2 and report results, and the company has published on the timeline from target to clinical candidate being much shorter than the industry norm. It has several other programmes in clinical trials and has licensed candidates to larger companies. The results so far are encouraging for the method but do not yet include an approved medicine, which is the only test that settles the question.

Why the model is debated

Supporters see proof that AI can compress discovery. Sceptics note that the targets and molecules still pass through the same clinical trials as any other, where most drugs fail for reasons AI did not address, and that one company's timelines are hard to compare with industry averages. Both agree on what to watch: whether the later stage trials succeed, and whether the approach produces a stream of candidates rather than a single notable one. Insilico's answer to that will shape how much the industry invests in integrated platforms versus specialised tools.
